visuals.heading: Build a Sponsor, Not Just a Mentor

items.text: A mentor talks to you, advice, feedback, encouragement in a one-on-one conversation.
That is not a cynical take, it is a documented pattern.

blocks.heading: Good Work Is Not the Whole Answer

items.text: Most people are told that consistent output is what gets rewarded, and at a basic level that is true, you cannot get promoted on visibility alone if the underlying work is weak.
Promotion decisions are made in rooms you are not in, by people who cannot personally verify every project you shipped, every fire you put out, or every stakeholder you managed well.

blocks.heading: Single Clearest Lever in the Research

items.text: Harvard Business Review's research on this distinction, led by Herminia Ibarra and colleagues, found that without active sponsorship, even high-potential employees are meaningfully less likely to get promoted, and that sponsorship influence outweighs gender, personality, education, and experience combined in predicting who actually moves up.
Gives you advice, reviews your work, tells you what to improve.

blocks.heading: Deliberate Delay or Genuinely Not Ready

items.text: This is the question that eats the most time and energy for people stuck at the same level for two or three cycles in a row: is this a real gap, or is the promotion being quietly deferred without anyone saying so directly.
A genuine gap has a name: a specific skill, a rating threshold, a scope you have not yet owned.

blocks.heading: Pick Scope That Maps to the Next

items.text: A stretch project nobody knew was a test does not build a promotion case, it just becomes unpaid extra work.
Close the loop with evidence, not a request.

blocks.heading: Promotion Timelines Differ By Sector in India

items.text: IT services and product companies usually run structured annual cycles with defined levels, calibration meetings, and competency matrices, the sponsor and timing moves above map closely to how these companies actually decide.

BFSI and large corporates often add a formal role or grade evaluation layer, so scope expansion needs to be tied to a documented role change, not just informal extra work that never gets logged anywhere.

Government and PSU roles typically promote on seniority, departmental exams, and fixed cadres rather than manager sponsorship, so exam preparation and tenure planning matter more than the sponsor-and-visibility playbook here.

Startups and smaller companies often have no formal calibration process at all, so a direct, evidence-backed conversation with your manager or founder can move faster than waiting for a cycle that may not exist yet.

blocks.heading: Mistakes That Slow the Promotion Down Further

items.text: Assuming the work speaks for itself.
Collecting mentors instead of building a sponsor.
Asking right after calibration has closed.
Taking on stretch work without naming the goal.
Accepting a vague "not yet" for multiple cycles without asking for specifics.
